analysis.one_liner: Requires deep cuts in mercury pollution from coal plants, incinerators, cement kilns, and consumer products.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a committee vote or floor action in the Senate and died when the 109th Congress ended in January 2007.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required steep reductions in mercury emissions from coal-fired power plants, industrial boilers, waste incinerators, chlor-alkali chemical plants, and cement plants, and would have phased mercury out of everyday products like batteries and fluorescent bulbs. Mercury from these sources settles into water, builds up in fish, and poses neurological risks to developing babies — in 2003, 45 states warned residents about eating contaminated fish [S3]. The bill was introduced by Sen. Patrick Leahy of Vermont, with Sen. Olympia Snowe of Maine as its only cosponsor [S4], and was referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee, where it sat without any further action through the end of the Congress [S1][S5].
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, the main beneficiaries would have been pregnant women, infants, children, and people who eat a lot of freshwater fish — the groups the bill identifies as most at risk from mercury [S3]. It also would have lowered mercury exposure for anyone living near coal plants or incinerators, and required public reporting of facility-by-facility mercury emissions, letting residents see what their neighborhood plants release [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Pregnant women, children, and fish eaters

how_it_helps.text: Requires coal-fired power plants to meet an emission rate of no more than 2.48 grams of mercury per 1,000 megawatt hours starting in 2009, with a national cap of 5 tons of mercury per year by 2010 [S3].
Requires 90% reductions in mercury from coal- and oil-fired industrial boilers, and 95% reductions at chlor-alkali chemical plants and Portland cement plants [S3].

Mandates that mercury-containing items like fluorescent bulbs, batteries, thermostats, and medical instruments be separated from the waste stream, labeled, and preferably recycled, and phases out the sale of mercury-containing products without an exemption [S2][S3].

Requires permanent disposal of captured mercury so it does not re-enter the environment, bans sale of the mercury in the National Defense Stockpile, and expands nationwide mercury deposition monitoring [S3].
Requires EPA to make facility-specific mercury emission data public every year and to improve the consistency of state fish-consumption advisories [S3].

analysis.who_pays: The costs would fall on coal-fired electricity generators, which would need to install and run mercury control equipment and accept a hard national cap; on chlor-alkali chemical plants, cement kilns, and waste incinerators, which face 95% or equivalent reductions; and on manufacturers of mercury-containing products, which would have to label, take back, or redesign them [S3]. Some of these costs could be passed through to electricity customers and to prices of cement, chemicals, and consumer goods [S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Coal plants, cement kilns, chemical makers

drawbacks.text: Mercury control retrofit costs at hundreds of power plants would likely be passed through to electricity customers and raise prices for cement, chlor-alkali chemicals, and wallboard, an honest supporter would have to acknowledge [S3].

The blanket phaseout of mercury-containing products three years after enactment could disrupt legitimate uses — like fluorescent lamps and some medical or scientific instruments — until the EPA exemption process, which requires showing no reasonable-cost mercury-free alternative, sorts out which products are truly essential [S3].

Requiring near-total (90-95%) emission reductions across so many source types on short timelines could force plant closures or fuel switching in communities dependent on those facilities for jobs [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The health stakes are large and one-sided: the bill's own findings cite the National Academy of Sciences and CDC data showing roughly 630,000 newborns a year at risk of neurological effects from prenatal mercury exposure, and mercury advisories in fish nearly tripled from 1993 to 2003 [S3]. The compliance costs are real and would show up partly in electricity and manufactured-goods prices, but the bill allowed facility-level averaging and trading within sites and gave EPA flexibility in setting standards, which softens the expense [S3]. On balance it was a serious, if aggressive, public-health bill whose main costs fell on polluting industries rather than being charged directly to the public.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate sent the bill to the Environment and Public Works Committee the day it was introduced, and it stayed there — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote — until the Congress ended in January 2007 [S1][S5].

narrative.text: Sen. Patrick Leahy introduced the Mercury Emission Act of 2005 on April 6, 2005, with Sen. Olympia Snowe as its sole cosponsor, making it bipartisan from the start [S3][S4].
The same day, the Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Environment and Public Works [S1][S5].
The committee took no further action — no markup, no report — and the bill never reached the Senate floor before the 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007 [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Coal-fired power plants, chlor-alkali plants, cement kilns, and incinerator operators were better off, because they avoided mandatory deep mercury cuts, monitoring, permit requirements, and public disclosure of their emissions. Mercury-containing product manufacturers also avoided a mandated phaseout. The public gained nothing, since the health protections never took effect.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Coal plants and other mercury emitters

sides.party_line_note: The bill was bipartisan in sponsorship — a Vermont Democrat joined by Maine Republican Olympia Snowe — but it never came to a vote, and the Republican-controlled committee that could have moved it took no action [S4][S5].

industries.note: Their plants were the largest single source of U.S. mercury emissions under the bill's own findings, and the bill imposed a hard 5-ton national cap plus rate limits and mandatory controls. Avoiding those controls saved the industry substantial retrofit costs that would otherwise have cut into profits, while the public continued absorbing the health costs through contaminated fish.
Plants using the mercury cell process would have had to cut mercury emissions 95%, adding costs to a production method that releases mercury into the environment.
Cement kilns would have faced 95% mercury reductions and permits, raising production costs for an industry whose kilns also emit mercury from burning fuels and raw materials.
The bill set a strict mercury emission rate for incinerators, required monitoring and permits, and forced separation of mercury-containing items before burning or landfilling.

industries.industry: Mercury-containing product manufacturers (batteries, fluorescent lamps, switches)
industries.note: They faced labeling, take-back, and a three-year sales phaseout unless exempted, a real compliance burden. But the rules targeted mercury content, not the industries' underlying business, and firms able to redesign or get exemptions could continue selling.

industries.industry: Coal combustion waste users (wallboard and cement makers, agricultural users)
industries.note: The bill banned agricultural application of coal combustion waste and limited emissions from reprocessing it, closing off a low-cost disposal route that shifts mercury back into the environment.
